decks.title: Money Smarts · Little
decks.description: Needs vs wants, saving jar, price tags, making change

cards.front: Is candy a need or a want?
cards.back: Candy is a want.

cards.front: What does $3 on a price tag mean?
cards.back: $3 means the item costs 3 dollars.

cards.front: Can you save money in a piggy bank?
cards.back: Yes, putting coins in a jar helps save money.

cards.front: How do you make change for $1?
cards.back: Use pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters to reach 1 dollar.

cards.front: Should I share my toys or keep them all?
cards.back: Sharing is nice but you can also decide which ones to keep.

cards.front: Can I earn money by helping at home?
cards.back: Yes, doing chores like cleaning up can earn allowance.

cards.front: Is a toy car a need or want?
cards.back: A toy car is a want.
Count them as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 to make 5 cents.

cards.front: Is a sandwich a need or want?
cards.back: A sandwich is a need for food.

cards.front: Can I buy two toys with $2?
cards.back: Only if the two toys together cost $2 or less.

cards.front: Is a new shirt a need or want?
cards.back: Clothes can be a need. An extra fancy shirt is usually a want.
Count them as 10, 20, 30 to make 30 cents.

cards.front: Should I spend all my money at once?
cards.back: It's better to save some for later needs or wants.

cards.front: Can I earn more by doing extra chores?
cards.back: Yes, talk with parents about earning more allowance.

cards.front: Is a new game a need or want?
cards.back: A new game is usually a want.
Count them as 25, 50, 75, 100 to make 1 dollar.

cards.front: Should I share my snacks with friends?
cards.back: Sharing is kind but you can keep some for yourself too.

cards.front: Can I earn money by helping neighbors?
cards.back: Yes, doing small jobs like raking leaves can earn allowance.

cards.front: Is a new crayon set a need or want?
cards.back: A new crayon set is usually a want unless it's very old.
Count them as 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 to make 25 cents.

decks.title: Money Smarts · Middle
decks.description: Budgeting, simple interest, comparing prices, unit price

cards.back: A job is work you do to earn money.
Chores are tasks at home that help keep things clean and tidy.
Saving money helps you buy things later or in case of emergencies.
A budget is a plan that shows how much money you have and where it goes.
Separate your money into jars for giving to others, saving for later, or spending now.
Interest is extra money you earn when you keep money in a savings account.

cards.front: Simple interest example: $100 at 5% for 1 year
cards.back: $100 × 0.05 × 1 year = $5 interest. You would have $105.
Look at the price tag and decide if it's worth what you pay.
Unit price tells you how much one item costs, like per ounce or per pound.

cards.front: Which cereal is cheaper: $3 for 12oz or $4 for 16oz?
cards.back: $3 for 12oz = $0.25/oz; $4 for 16oz = $0.25/oz; Both are the same price per ounce.
Goals help you decide what to save money for and work towards them.
It's waiting to buy something now so you can have more later.

cards.front: Simple interest example: $50 at 4% for 2 years
cards.back: $50 at 4% simple interest for 2 years earns $4 total ($50 × 0.04 × 2 = $4). About $2 per year.
You can earn money by doing jobs or chores around the house.
A place where you keep your saved coins and money safe.
It helps you remember what you want to buy with your savings.

cards.front: Simple interest example: $20 at 3% for 5 years
cards.back: $20 × 0.03 × 5 years = $3 interest total ($0.60 per year).
A place where you keep your money safe and earn interest.
Saving for unexpected things helps you feel secure and not worry.
A card that lets you spend money from your bank account.
It helps you know where your money goes and if you have enough left over.
A card that lets you borrow money to buy things, but must be paid back.

cards.front: Simple interest example: $150 at 6% for 3 years
cards.back: $150 × 0.06 × 3 years = $27 interest total ($9 per year).
A bank account where you can deposit and withdraw money easily.

decks.title: Money Smarts · Older
decks.description: Compound interest, credit, scams, inflation, Bitcoin basics (neutral)

cards.back: Interest earned on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods.

cards.front: Example of compound interest: $100 at 10% compounded yearly for 2 years
cards.back: Year 1: $100 × 1.10 = $110. Year 2: $110 × 1.10 = $121. You earned $21 total (more than $20 simple interest).

cards.front: How does credit card interest work?
cards.back: Interest is charged on unpaid balances each month.

cards.front: Example: $100 balance, 20% APR, paid off in one month
cards.back: Monthly rate ≈ 20% ÷ 12 = 1.667%. One month on $100 ≈ $1.67 if no grace period. Pay in full during the grace period and you owe $0 interest.
Fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information by disguising as a trustworthy entity in electronic communication.

cards.front: Red flag: Unsolicited request for gift cards
cards.back: Legitimate organizations do not ask for payment via gift card.
Increase in prices over time, reducing the purchasing power of money.

cards.front: Example: $1 candy bar now costs $2 due to inflation
cards.back: If a candy bar cost $1 last year and now costs $2, it's an example of inflation.
A medium of exchange that allows people to buy goods and services. It also stores value over time.
Bitcoin is digital money recorded on a public network. Supply is limited by design. This is a description, not advice to buy or sell.

cards.front: Why does Bitcoin have a volatile price?
cards.back: Supply and demand in the market can cause large fluctuations.

cards.front: Is Bitcoin issued by any government?
cards.back: No, it is decentralized and not controlled by any single entity or country.

cards.front: What does APR mean on a credit card?
cards.back: Annual Percentage Rate — the yearly cost of borrowing if you carry a balance.

cards.front: If you only pay the minimum on a credit card, what happens?
cards.back: The leftover balance keeps earning interest, so the debt can grow and take much longer to pay off.

cards.front: Compound vs simple: $100 at 10% for 2 years
cards.back: Simple: $100 + $10 + $10 = $120. Compound yearly: $121. The extra $1 is interest on interest.

cards.front: Red flag: a message says 'act now or your account will be locked' with a link
cards.back: Pressure + unexpected link is a common phishing trick. Go to the real site yourself instead of tapping the link.

cards.front: Red flag: someone asks you to pay with gift cards or crypto to 'fix a problem'
cards.back: Real companies and agencies do not collect that way. It is a scam.

cards.front: Red flag: an offer that promises guaranteed huge returns with no risk
cards.back: If it sounds too good to be true, it usually is. High return always pairs with risk.
How many goods or services your money can buy. Inflation lowers purchasing power over time.

cards.front: If prices rise 5% in a year and your cash earns 1%, what happened?
cards.back: Your cash buys less than before. 5% inflation vs 1% interest means you lost about 4% in buying power.
1) Medium of exchange (you trade it for stuff). 2) Unit of account (prices). 3) Store of value (hold for later).
Money you borrowed and must pay back, often with interest.

cards.front: Good habit before using a credit card
cards.back: Have a plan to pay the statement balance in full each month so interest does not start.
No single company or government issues it. Changes need wide agreement across the network. Still: not buy/sell advice.

cards.front: Bitcoin: what does volatile mean here?
cards.back: The price can jump up or down a lot in short times. That risk is part of why it is not the same as cash in a bank.

cards.front: What is a budget for a teen?
cards.back: A written plan for income (job, gifts) split into save / spend / give, reviewed each month.
Cash set aside for surprise needs (broken phone, lost shift) so you do not need high-interest debt.

cards.front: Unit price check: $6 for 20 oz vs $4 for 12 oz — which is cheaper per oz?
cards.back: $6/20 = $0.30 per oz. $4/12 ≈ $0.333 per oz. The 20 oz option is cheaper per ounce.
